lines.text: Dev says nobody tells him what to CHOOSE.
Theo bets him three FACTS say otherwise.
Fact one. If people must opt in as organ donors, 42 PERCENT do.
If they must opt out? 82 PERCENT.
Fact two. 24 jams: 3 percent bought. Six jams? 30 PERCENT.
But later studies say that one doesn't always HOLD.
Fact three. Add a worse copy of one option, and the original looks BETTER.
Dev laughs. Then buys the large popcorn, because the medium cost almost the SAME.

post.title: 3 Facts About How You Decide #shorts
post.description: Dev says nobody tells him what to choose. Theo bets him three facts. 1) Defaults: in an online experiment by Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein (2003, "Do Defaults Save Lives?", Science), 42% agreed to be organ donors when they had to opt in, but 82% stayed donors when they had to opt out. 2) Choice overload: in Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper's 2000 jam study, about 3% of shoppers who stopped at a 24-jam table bought jam, versus about 30% at a 6-jam table, though a later meta-analysis of 50 studies (Scheibehenne, Greifeneder & Todd, 2010) found the effect is not reliable. 3) The decoy effect (Huber, Payne & Puto, 1982): adding a worse version of one option makes that option look better. Psychologists call the way options are set up choice architecture. #psychology #shorts #decisions #marketing
